## Methods

Isolation of pure AOB strain
Surface sediment samples (0–2 cm) were collected from the mud flat in a mangrove wetland in Zhanjiang Bay in November 2020 (Supplementary Fig. 1c). The sediment samples were placed in a cooler and transported to the laboratory for the enrichment and isolation of AOB. Detailed procedures for AOB enrichment and isolation processes are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1a. Briefly, ~2 g of sediment samples were added into 40 mL AOB enrichment medium54, and the resulting mixture was incubated at 30 °C with shaking at 120 rpm in the dark until a high ammonia oxidation rate was detected. Subsequently, a small volume of the enriched culture was transferred to a culture flask containing fresh medium (10% inoculation) for further cultivation until ammonium depletion. The dilution procedure was repeated multiple times until no culturable heterotrophic microorganisms were detected using nutrient agar. The abundances of AOB and total bacteria in these enrichments were quantified based on quantitative PCR of the β-AOB amoA55 and bacterial 16S rRNA genes56, respectively. When AOB accounted for ≥90% of the total bacteria, the enrichment culture was diluted and then inoculated onto AOB solid medium (2% agar)54. A single colony was selected and isolated for further study. Finally, we obtained a pure AOB strain whose 16S rRNA gene sequence exhibited high sequence similarity (>98.8% identity) to that of isolated N. halophila Nm11 and formed a distinct cluster with N. halophila Nm1 in the phylogenetic tree (Supplementary Fig. 1d). Given its sampling location, this pure AOB isolate is named N. halophila ZJB1 (Zhangjiang Bay).

The phylogenetic tree of the AOB 16S rRNA gene
The 16S rRNA gene sequences of representative AOB were retrieved from GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) for phylogenetic analyses. These sequences were arrayed with MAFFT-L-INS-I57 and pruned using BMGE (BLOSUM30)58. Maximum-likelihood tree was inferred with IQ-TREE under GTR+F+I+G4 model59. Ultrafast bootstrapping (1000 replicates) was used.

Phylogenies of AmoD and AmoE sequences
The AmoE sequence from N. halophila ZJB1 was used as a query to search against the nr database using BLASTP60, and hits with >50% amino acid similarity were downloaded. For AmoD phylogeny, the bacterial sequences containing the lipoprotein family motif of AmoD (PS51257) were downloaded from the Interpro database (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/search/sequence/). After excluding proteins longer than 100 amino acids, a total of 474 homologous sequences were obtained. These sequences were aligned with MAFFT-L-INS-I57 and pruned using BMGE (BLOSUM30)58. Maximum-likelihood trees were inferred with IQ-TREE (cpREV+G4 for AmoD; WAG+G4 for AmoE; -bb 1000)59.

Chemical analyses
Ammonium and nitrite concentrations were measured using the optimized indophenol blue method61 and the modified Griess-Llosvay procedure62, respectively. Briefly, 100 μL of culture or buffer was aliquoted into sterile 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes and centrifuged at 15,000×g for 5 min at room temperature to pellet large particulates and cells. The supernatant was transferred to fresh sterile 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes and diluted to a final volume of 1 mL with NH +-free ultrapure water. For the optimized indophenol blue assay, 50 μL of phenol-nitroprusside solution and 50 μL of alkaline hypochlorite solution were added; alternatively, for the modified Griess-Llosvay assay, 50 μL of sulfanilamide solution and 50 μL of naphthylamine solution were used. Following complete color development, absorbance was measured at 630 nm for ammonium and at 543 nm for nitrite using a microplate reader (EnSpire). Final concentrations were calculated using standard curves for NH +(0–10 μM, n=3, R2>0.998) and NO -(0-20 μM, n=3, R2>0.999), respectively.

DNA extraction, gene cloning, and plasmid construction
DNA was extracted from 2 mL culture using the PowerSoil® DNA Isolation kit (MoBio Laboratories, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The DNA concentrations were measured using the NanoValue™ Plus micro nucleic acid analyzer (GE Healthcare Life, Pittsburgh, PA, USA). The PCR primers used in this study are shown in Supplementary Table 2.
(i) pJTU1278 (Catalog No. TSPLA16579, Ningbo Testa Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), a plasmid used for the construction of a suicide vector harboring the KmR gene. The recombinant suicide plasmid consists of three fragments: the first fragment (2.9 kb) was PCR amplified using the primer pair pJTU-F/pJTU-R, incorporating the ori, lacZ, and AmpR genes from the pJTU1278 plasmid63 along with an XbaI restriction site. The second fragment (558 bp) was PCR amplified using the primer pair oriT-F/oriT-R, containing the conjugative ori and the traJ gene. The third fragment, a kanamycin resistance gene (KmR)64, was synthesized by GENEWIZ Biotechnology Co., LTD (Suzhou, China) and PCR amplified using the primer pair KmR-F/KmR-R, resulting in a 978 bp product that includes the KmR promoter. Subsequently, the three fragments were assembled into the plasmid, pJTU1278-KmR, using the ClonExpress Ultra One Step Cloning Kit V2 (Vazyme, Nanjing, China).
(ii) pJTU1278-KmR, a plasmid used for the assembly of amoCAB genes and fusion tags. A 1.42 kb DNA fragment encompassing the amoC gene and its promoter sequence from N. halophila ZJB1 was amplified by PCR using primers amoC-F/amoC-R, with the reverse primer amoC-R containing a XbaI restriction site and Strep-Tag II fusion tag. The resulting PCR products were purified via gel extraction and ligated into the XbaI site of the vector, followed by transformation into E. coli DH5α cells. Similarly, the amoA (1.08 kb) and amoB (1.28 kb) genes were PCR amplified using respective primer pairs amoA-F/amoA-R and amoB-F/amoB-R. The corresponding PCR products were also gel-purified and ligated into the XbaI site before being transformed into E. coli DH5α cells. In addition, 3×Flag fusion tag was introduced downstream of amoA via reverse primers. Ultimately, we successfully constructed an 8253 bp suicide plasmid, designated as pJTU1278-KmR-AMO.

Electroporation-mediated cell transformation
N. halophila ZJB1 cells (1 L) from an early-stationary-phase liquid culture (OD ≈0.2) were harvested by centrifugation and washed three times with sterile water. The sedimented cells were resuspended in 1.5 mL of sterile water and kept on ice until use. Electroporation was carried out using an ECM399 Electroporation System (BTX Harvard Apparatus, voltage range of 60-2500 V, fixed capacitance of 36 μF, fixed resistance of 150 Ω). Aliquots (100 μL) of electrocompetent cells were transformed with 5 μL plasmid DNA (1 μg DNA/μL) in 1 mm gap parallel electrode cuvettes (Fisherbrand) at a constant voltage of 1.2 kV. A control for the electroporation experiment consisted of cell aliquots without added DNA. Immediately after electroporation, the cells were transferred to 200 mL of fresh medium and incubated for 24 h under nonselective conditions at 30 °C with shaking (100 rpm). Kanamycin was then added to a final concentration of 25 μg/mL. Cell growth was monitored by measuring consumption of NH + and accumulation of NO -. Finally, a small volume of cultures was transferred to a culture flask with fresh medium (10% inoculation) containing kanamycin (25 μg/mL) for further culturing until NH + was depleted. This process was repeated, and after two months, kanamycin-resistant cultures were successfully obtained.

AMO purification
120 L N. halophila ZJB1 cells expressing AmoA-Flag were harvested by vacuum filtration through a 0.22 μM pore polycarbonate membrane filter (Millipore). The collected cells were subsequently resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM PIPES pH 7.2, 50 mM NaCl, 30 μM CuSO ) and lysed by sonication on ice. The lysate was then supplemented with n-Decyl-β-D-Malyranoside (DDM) to a final concentration of 2%, followed by stirring for 2 h at 4 °C to extract the membrane proteins. Subsequently, cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 20,000×g for 30 mins at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant was collected and incubated with anti-FLAG beads for 2 h at 4 °C. The beads were washed extensively by SEC buffer (50 mM PIPES pH 7.2, 50 mM NaCl, 30 μM CuSO , 0.06% digitonin (DIG)). Proteins were eluted by 200 μg/mL 3×FLAG peptide in the SEC buffer. The eluent was loaded onto a Superose S6 3.2/60 column (GE Healthcare) equilibrated with SEC buffer. Peak fractions were collected for cryo-EM sample preparation.

Activity assays
The ammonia oxidation activity was measured separately using intact AOB cells, cell lysates (either centrifuged supernatant or non-centrifuged suspension), membrane fractions, and purified AMO protein. Briefly, N. halophila ZJB1 was cultured to the late exponential growth phase, and approximately 3 g of cells were harvested via filtration through a 0.22 μm membrane filter (Millipore). The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in 50 mL of SEC buffer (OD ≈5.0) and aliquoted into sterile 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes (1 mL per tube). Cell disruption was carried out using an ultrasonic disruptor (Xinzhi Instrument, Zhejiang, China) under the following conditions: 80 W power output, with a 2 s pulse followed by a 4 s pause, for a total duration of 3 min. The disrupted cell suspension was either used directly as the non-centrifuged cell lysate or further processed by centrifugation. For preparation of the centrifuged extract, the lysate was centrifuged at 2000×g at 4 °C for 20 min to remove intact cells and large cellular debris. Total protein concentration was determined using a micro-UV spectrophotometer (Bio-Rad). The non-centrifuged lysate exhibited a protein concentration of approximately 22.3 mg/mL, whereas the centrifuged supernatant showed a reduced concentration of 12.1 mg/mL—approximately half that of the non-centrifuged sample. To account for this loss during centrifugation, twice the initial biomass was used in the preparation of centrifuged extracts to ensure equivalent protein loading in downstream assays.
For the membrane fractions, ~3 g of N. halophila ZJB1 cell pellet was carried to ultrasonic disruption. The resulting lysate was centrifuged at 21,500×g and 4 °C for 10 min. The supernatant was collected and then ultracentrifuged at 150,000×g and 4 °C for 1 h. After discarding the final supernatant, the membrane pellet was resuspended in 10 mL of SEC buffer. The total protein concentration of this membrane fractions was determined to be 9.5 mg/mL. Given that the AMO protein constitutes approximately 80% of the total membrane protein65, the estimated AMO protein concentration in this membrane fractions was about 7.6 mg/mL. The AMO protein was purified according to the method described above in this study, yielding a final concentration of ~3.0 mg/mL.
To investigate the factors influencing AMO activity, a series of reductants was evaluated using intact AOB cells and cell lysates. The reductants tested included duroquinone (5 mM), formate (26 mM), and NADH (10 mM), which have been widely employed as effective electron donors for measuring pMMO activity in methanotrophs28,30,66,67. In addition, the effects of several potential reductants or electron donors on the ammonia oxidation activity of intact cells and cell lysates were investigated, including ubiquinol (CoQ H , 50 μM), sodium ascorbate (Asc., 10 mM), DL-dithiothreitol (DTT, 10 mM), and tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP, 10 mM). In reductant or electron donor assays, 1 mL of intact cell suspension or cell suspension or cell lysate was transferred to a 10 mL centrifuge tube. To this, 1 mL of SEC buffer, NH ⁺ (~5 mM), KH PO (12 mM), NaHCO (13 mM), and essential trace metals for AOB (1 mL/L) were added. A negative control without any reductant was included in each experimental series. For activity assays using membrane fractions and purified AMO protein, 1 mL of sample was transferred into 10 mL centrifuge tubes; the membrane fractions were subsequently supplemented with 1 mL of SEC buffer to achieve a final volume of 2 mL. The reaction mixtures were supplemented with CoQ H (50 μM), NH ⁺ (~5 mM), KH PO (12 mM), NaHCO (13 mM), and essential trace metals for AOB (1 mL/L). A blank control containing CoQ H but lacking membrane fractions or purified AMO protein was also included. All assays were incubated in the dark at 30 °C with shaking at 120 rpm in a temperature-controlled incubator. Aliquots were collected at predetermined time intervals to measure NH ⁺ consumption, allowing for the monitoring of ammonia oxidation activity.

Construction of mutants and enzyme activity assays
DNA fragments containing point mutations at specific amino acid residues associated with Cu and Cu were generated. Briefly, PCR amplification was carried out using the primers listed in Supplementary Table 2, and the resulting PCR products were purified. Following the cloning procedure described previously in this study, the mutated DNA fragments were initially ligated into a kanamycin resistance gene-free pJTU1278 vector to reconstruct the complete amoC gene. Subsequently, a kanamycin resistance cassette (KmR) and the amoA gene were inserted downstream through ligation. A final PCR was then performed using the primer pair amoC-F1/amoA-R1, and the amplified product was purified to yield the full-length mutated DNA fragment. The constructed fragments were introduced into the N. halophila ZJB1 wild-type strain via electroporation as described above. Transformants were selected on agar plates supplemented with 25 mg/L kanamycin, yielding six kanamycin-resistant mutant strains.
Ammonia oxidation activity of the mutant strains was assessed by monitoring NH + consumption over time. In brief, each mutant culture was adjusted to an OD of approximately 0.06 and transferred into AOB growth medium to a final volume of 10 mL, with NH + provided at a final concentration of ~2 mM along with other essential nutrients required for AOB growth. Cultures were incubated at 30 °C under shaking conditions (120 rpm). Aliquots were collected at regular intervals to determine NH + concentrations, allowing for the evaluation of ammonia oxidation activity in each mutant.

Lipidomics analysis
The lipid extraction and LC-MS/MS analysis for N. halophila ZJB1 cells and purified AMO protein were performed for three independent biological replicates, respectively. Internal standards, including TG (16:0-d9/16:0/16:0), SM (d18:1/16:0-d9), DG (16:0-d9/16:0), CE (16:0-d9), PC (16:0-d9/16:0), PE (16:0-d9/16:0), PI (16:0-d9/16:0), PS (16:0-d9/16:0) and LysoPC (16:0-d9/0:0), were added to N. halophila ZJB1 cells and AMO protein samples suspended in 1 mL of phosphate-buffered saline:methanol (1:1, v/v). The mixture was homogenized using a Precellys homogenizer (Retsch) through three cycles of 30 s at 8000 rpm, with 5 min incubations on ice between each cycle.
A methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE)-based liquid-liquid extraction method was subsequently performed. Four milliliters of MTBE were added to each sample and vortexed vigorously. The mixtures were incubated for 1 h at room temperature on a platform shaker (Shanghai Jinsin Technology Co., Ltd.) operating at 500 rpm. Phase separation was achieved by the addition of 1 mL of water. After shaking for 10 min, the samples were centrifuged at 2000×g for 15 min. The upper organic phase from each sample was carefully aspirated using a Pasteur pipette and transferred to a fresh glass tube. The residual aqueous phase was subjected to a second extraction with 2.5 mL of MTBE/methanol/water (10:3:2.5, v/v/v). Following the same shaking and centrifugation steps as described above, the resulting organic phase was collected and combined with the initial extract. The lipid extracts were dried under a stream of nitrogen using a SpeedVac vacuum concentrator. The dried lipids were reconstituted in 200 μL of n-butanol/methanol (1:1, v/v) and transferred to autosampler vials for lipidomic profiling via LC-MS (ExionLC™ AD, SCIEX) tandem MS (QTRAP 6500+, SCIEX).
The LC-MS analytical conditions were as follows: HPLC column, Shim-pack VP-ODS C18 (pore size 5.0 μm, dimensions 2×150 mm); mobile phase, water containing 0.04% acetic acid and acetonitrile containing 0.04% acetic acid; gradient program, 100:0 (v/v) at 0 min, 5:95 (v/v) at 20.0 min, 5:95 (v/v) at 22.0 min, 95:5 (v/v) at 22.1 min, and 95:5 (v/v) at 28.0 min; flow rate, 0.25 mL min⁻¹; column temperature, 40 °C; injection volume, 5 μL. The eluate was alternately directed to an electrospray ionization triple quadrupole–linear ion trap (QTRAP)–MS or an electrospray ionization QqTOF–MS. The mass spectrometer was operated under the following conditions: ion source temperature, 500 °C; ion spray voltage, +5500 V in positive mode and −4500 V in negative mode; nebulizing gas 1 (GS1), 45 psi; auxiliary gas 2 (GS2), 55 psi; curtain gas, 35 psi. In the triple quadrupole mode, each precursor-product ion pair was monitored using optimized declustering potentials and collision energies.
All mass spectrometry data were acquired and processed using the Xcalibur 3.0 software suite. Lipid annotation and data processing were performed using Lipostar software (version 1.3.1b18; Molecular Discovery). Feature detection, noise and artifact filtering, retention time alignment, and lipid identification were conducted. Peak picking, signal smoothing and alignment algorithms were applied to resolve unique m/z and retention time pairs. A retention time window of 1–32 min was implemented during analysis. Background signals arising from blank solvents, features lacking MS/MS spectra, peaks without detectable isotopic patterns, and nonspecific noise were excluded from further analysis.
The identification and quantification of lipid molecular species were performed using LipidSearch software (version 4.1; Mitsui Knowledge Industry, Tokyo, Japan). The key processing parameters were configured as follows: target database, LIPID MAPS; precursor ion mass tolerance, 5 ppm; production mass tolerance, 5 ppm; product ion intensity threshold, 5%; m-score threshold, 1; quantitative m/z tolerance, ±5 ppm; quantitative retention time (RT) window, ±0.5 min; application of the main isomer filter and ID quality filters A, B, C, and D; adductions included +H and +NH₄⁺ in positive ion mode, and –H, +HCOO⁻, and –2H in negative ion mode. The major lipid classes selected for the search including glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, diacylglycerols, triacylglycerols and sterols—in both positive and negative ionization modes. Identified lipids were assigned confidence scores on a 1- to 4-star scale, with higher ratings indicating greater identification certainty. Only identifications rated at 2 stars or above were retained for downstream analysis. The integrated peak areas of all identified lipids were normalized to those of their respective class-specific internal standards. For the five most abundant molecular species within each lipid class—ranked by normalized peak area ratios—identifications were manually validated and confirmed through careful inspection of MS/MS fragmentation patterns and chromatographic peak profiles.

Negative stain
4 μL purified AMO sample was applied onto the freshly plasma glow-discharged carbon grids (30 sec at 15 mA current) and stained with 2% uranyl acetate twice for 60 sec each. Images were taken with a FEI Morgagni transmission electron microscope at a magnification of 730,000× under a defocus value of ~−1.5 um.

Preparation and data acquisition of cryo-EM sample
For cryo-EM sample preparation, the Au grids (Quantifoil, R2/1, 300 mesh) coated with single-layered graphene (gifted by Jiayue Su, Tsinghua University) were used to address the issue of AMO particles failing to enter the grid holes. The grids underwent glow discharge treatment (10 mA, 10 sec) and mounted on forceps in a Mark IV Vitrobot (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 4 °C and 100% humidity. A volume of 5 μL of the fresh AMO samples were floated on the grid for 15 sec, after which the grid was plunge-frozen in liquid ethane following blotting. Cryo-EM data of AMO was collected on a Titan Krios electron microscope operating at 300 kV, equipped with a Gatan K3 Summit direct electron detector and a GIF Quantum energy filter. The automatic software-EPU68 was used for data acquisition. Images were recorded at a pixel size of 0.668 Å under a magnification of 130,000×. The defocus value of each image was set from −1.5 to −2.0 μm during data collection. Each micrograph was dose-fractioned into 32 frames with a total dose of about 50 e–/Å2.

Image processing
The beam-induced motion of the whole micrograph was corrected by MotionCor2 1.1.069. All the following data processing procedures were carried out in cryoSPARC 4.3.270. Contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were estimated by Patch CTF estimation for the AMO, and micrographs with poor CTF fit, as determined by Manually Curate Exposures were rejected. Particle picking was carried out using Blob Picker with diameter ranging from 8 to 20 nm. Auto-picked particles were extracted by a binning factor of 2. Following two-dimensional (2D) classification, good classes were used to train Topaz71. This dataset underwent additional rounds of 2D classification and Topaz train and extraction, repeating the process four times until no further improvements were observed. All particles from these iterations were combined, and duplicated particles were removed. A total of 382,927 particles were subjected to ab initio 3D reconstruction, followed by heterogeneous refinement to generate four EM maps. The map with AMO complex contained a total of 153,286 particles, which was subjected to two rounds of AMO heterogeneous refinement to remove the bad particles using the maps generated in the previous step as references. The best map was subsequently selected for further NU-refinement72, leading to an overall resolution of 2.36 Å as estimated by the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation at a correlation cutoff value of 0.14373. Finally, DeepEMhancer74 was employed for post-processing the final maps to facilitate model building.

Model building and refinement
The predicted AlphaFold structures of AmoA, AmoB, AmoC, AmoD, and AmoE were manually docked into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF Chimera 1.1275 and subsequently adjusted in Coot 0.8.9.176 according to the corresponding density and sequence information. Lipid molecules were selected based on lipidomic data and identifiable features, and were manually fitted into the map using Coot. Water molecules within the AMO complex, particularly those near copper centers, were modeled with reference to the previously reported pMMO structure (PDB: 7S4H) and supported by mass spectrometry data31. Additional cytoplasmic and periplasmic water molecules were placed based on the pMMO structure (PDB: 7S4H) and validated by the recently published AMO structure (PDB: 9CL6). Real-space refinement and validation of the final model were carried out using Phenix 1.14-3260,77. Structural figures were prepared with UCSF Chimera 1.1.2, ChimeraX 1.378, and PyMOL 1.8.2.1 (http://www.pymol.org).

Western blot
The western blot assays were performed following the standard procedure. Briefly, the purified AMO samples obtained from gel chromatography were resolved on a 4–20% SDS-PAGE (Yeasen Biotechnology) and transferred onto a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane. The membrane was then blocked with 5% skimmed milk in TBST buffer, followed by incubating with a suitable horseradish peroxidase (HRP) labeled primary antibody (Abclonal, Cat# AE024, 1:5000) for 2 h. Visualization of the blots was achieved using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit (Tanon), and images were captured using ChemiDoc™ MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad, CA, USA).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In their manuscript titled "Structural insights into the catalytic mechanism of ammonia monooxygenase", Yang and co-workers investigate the structure and mechanism of ammonia monooxygenase (AMO). Ammonia oxidation is the critical first step of the nitrification pathway witin the global nitrogen cycle, converting ammonia to hydroxylamine. AMO is an integral membrane metalloenzyme with high homology to particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) and is of ecological relevance, as it releases the greenhouse gas N2O, one of the main drivers of global warming, as a byproduct.
The authors successfully determined the cryo-EM structure of AMO from a newly isolated AOB strain, Nitrosomonas halophila ZJB1, at a resolution of 2.36 Å, yielding a complete atomic model including sidechains and – more importantly – the coordinated copper ions of the enzyme. The isolation and purification of the AOB strain and subsequently the AMO complex are detailed in the supplementary materials, including phylogenetic analysis of the isolated strain, the genetic engineering for purification, and the cryo-EM sample preparation and data processing. The data as presented seem sound and well processed, although the given initial number of particles (ca. 320,000) seems low for 6,000 micrographs, given the quality of the micrographs shown in Suppl. Fig. 2 and 3.
Like pMMO, AMO is a cylinder-shaped homotrimeric assembly of heteropentamers. Each protomer in the complex consists of five subunits: AmoA, AmoB, AmoC, a recently discovered single transmembrane protein (AmoD), and a newly identified extramembraneous subunit (AmoE). The core is composed of AmoA, AmoB, and AmoC, with AmoB forming periplasmic β-barrel domains arranged counterclockwise as a trimer. The structure is supported by 45 transmembrane helices contributed by each subunit in each protomer. This is ihe second report on a structure of AMO, with the first, at 2.8 Å resolution, determined in a native membrane environment by the group of Amy Rosenzweig in 2024 (listed as reference 25). This work had already identified the single-helix subunit that in the present work is now designated AmoD, but could not identifythe encoding gene due to a lack of resolution for the side chains. AmoD is a single transmembrane protein positioned adjacent to AmoC, with its N-terminus facing the cytoplasm and C-terminus oriented towards the periplasm. A similarly enigmatic helical structure has been observed in particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO), a related enzyme. Phylogenetic analysis suggests AmoD is exclusively present in the N. europaea/N. mobilis lineage and its genomic location is associated with genes involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and signaling molecule synthesis, leading the authors to the interesting proposal that it plays a role in signal transduction during ammonia oxidation. Two lipid molecules were observed embedded at the interface between AmoD and AmoC.
In addition, the present work identifies AmoE as a further accessory subunit, comprising two small helices and two flexible loops. AmoE binds to the positively-charged surface of the N-terminal cupredoxin domain of AmoB through electrostatic interactions. It also interacts with regions of AmoA and AmoC. Its genetic neighborhood includes genes encoding components of ATPase and outer membrane beta-barrel assembly machinery (BAM) complex. This led the authors to predict a probable involvement in facilitating the assembly of the AMO complex within the cell membrane. A speculative proposal, in particular because the connection of the (inner membrane protein) AMO to the BAM machinery is not clear to this reviewer.
The high-resolution structure of AMO revealed a total of nine copper-binding sites, with three per protomer forming two distinct copper centers. Interestingly, the dinuclear His-site (somewhat confusingly) designated CuA in some studies on pMMO, is not present in this AMO structure due to a substitution in the AmoB sequence, suggesting less conservation. CuB is considered to be an electron transfer site in pMMO, although a very similar site in the copper enzyme LPMO clearly is catalytic. In earlier work, the nuclearity of CuB has been under debate, but more recent data on pMMO already clarified its mononucler nature with the characteristic His-brace motif, and the present data on AMO now confirms this unambiguously. The active site of AMO is suggested to be at the CuC and CuD sites that feature a rather unique coordination environment for copper by including hard oxygen ligands from side chain carboxylates or amides. In AMO, the two sites form a second copper center with two simultaneously occupied copper ligands, contrasting with individual CuC and CuD sites proposed in some pMMO structures. These are nestled within a hydrophobic channel formed by transmembrane helices from AmoA and AmoC.
The authors also observe density features between CuC and CuD and model these as water molecules, which seems somewhat arbitrary given the map quality shown in Fig. 2c. Noting that in the AMO reaction the source of the oxygen atom of hydroxylamine is O2 rather than H2O, it seems that this now established dinuclear site would seem to be a great candidate for O2 activation similar to classical type III copper centers, and I suggest the authors may want to comment on this aspect of the mechanism. In contrast, they propose a rod-shaped density near CuC and CuD to be hydroxylamine or other intermediates, and this does not appear to be a strong point. In the map, the density feature is elongated and somewhat unclear, and quite clearly exceeds the dimensions of hydroxylamine, H2NOH, which at this resolution should present like a diatomic molecule with a compact density feature.
Furthermore, the authors elaborate on a water-mediated hydrogen-bonding network and suggesst that it constitutes an efficient electron transfer pathway from the periplasmic CuB to the active site CuC/CuD. Six water molecules and two key residues are involved in this pathway. Extensive lipid densities were observed within the AMO structure, their distribution and arrangement mirroring the native membrane environment, suggesting the particles were preserved in a functional state, although this structure is from an isolated enzyme rather than from a native lipid environment as in the case of the concurrently reported 2.8 Å structure of AMO from N. europaea by the Rosenzweig group (ref. 25). In a direct comparison, the authors now add the identification of AmoE and a detailed description of AmoD, defining AMO as a heteropentamer, distinct from archaeal AMO that seems to be an AmoABCXYZ heterohexamer. They furthermore resolve an occupied CuD site, defining a potential dinuclear active site that – again – might be discussed in relation to O2 activation. The higher resolution achieved (2.36 Å vs. 2.8 Å) seems to have been critical in resolving features like the presence of AmoE, the occupancy and coordination of the CuD site, and the detailed water network, thus providing a more comprehensive view of the proposed electron transfer pathway and active site.
In summary, this study represents a significant step forward in understanding the molecular architecture and catalytic mechanism of AMO by providing the most highly resolved and complete high-resolution cryo-EM structure. The determination of the complete heteropentameric composition, including the identification and proposed functional roles of AmoD and AmoE, adds crucial details to the understanding of this complex enzyme. The detailed mapping of copper centers, particularly the dinuclear CuC/CuD site, and the elucidation of the water-mediated electron transfer pathway provide a strong structural basis for the catalytic mechanism. Furthermore, the insights into the unique surface electrostatic potentials highlight possible mechanisms for substrate assimilation and transport. The study successfully integrates structural biology with bioinformatics and biochemical methods to provide a comprehensive view of AMO. The findings significantly enhance our understanding of this pivotal enzyme in the nitrogen cycle and its distinction from related enzymes like pMMO.

### Reviewer 2

Dong & Sui et al., titled "Structural insights into the catalytic mechanism of ammonia monooxygenase," reported their recent cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), a protein complex from ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB). In their research, the authors engineered the AmoA subdomain with a 3xFlag tag, co-expressed with the subunits of AmoB and AmoC, utilizing a heterogeneous vector. This construct was transformed and expressed in an AOB strain of Nitrosomonas halophila ZJB1. The resulting AmoABCDE membrane protein complexes were purified through an affinity column and subsequently collected for cryo-EM study.
In the cryo-EM study, the authors identified a periplasmic Cu(B) site in an AmoA subunit and a dinuclear copper (Cu(C) and Cu (D)) in an AmoC subunit. They proposed that the AMO complex facilitates ammonium oxidation through an effective electron transfer pathway from Cu(B) to the dinuclear copper site, enabling substrate oxidation. However, the study lacked direct evidence, unlike earlier studies published in the ref. 36 and 38, unequivocally demonstrating substrate binding, specifically ammonium or hydroxylamine, to the proposed dinuclear active site.
The copper sites of Cu(B), Cu(C), and Cu(D) have already been identified in various pMMO X-ray diffraction and cryo-EM structures. A recent cryoEM structure of AMO mentioned in the ref. 25 also revealed similar copper configurations for the Cu(B) and Cu(C) sites. Additionally, this study identified a corresponding Cu(D) site composed of Asn 207, His 211, and His 225, which may act as potential coordination ligands. Overall, the research progress achieved in this study is incremental.
The purified AMO complex is a heterogeneously expressed variant with a 3xFlag tag. It is necessary to perform a series of tests and characterizations related to AMO activity, including mechanistic and spectroscopic analyses, to verify that the obtained recombinant protein complex variants demonstrate AMO activity with high performance. The study also speculates on the potential structural differences between pMMO and AMO to provide mechanistic insights, although there is currently no strong evidence for these speculations. A more quantitative investigation is needed to achieve a fundamental understanding of how AMO facilitates biological ammonia oxidation at the molecular level. The results presented in this study are still preliminary, and this reviewer does not recommend the publication of the work in its present format.

### Reviewer 3

Yang et al., report a structure of an ammonia monooxygenase enzyme (AMO complex) from the ammonia-oxidising bacterium (AOB) Nitrosomonas halophila, and from a new strain that the authors isolated themselves from mangrove sediments. They have engineered a tagged version of the subunit Amo-A that they have used to isolate the full complex that they have analysed by cryo-EM. At the end of 2024, another group also obtained the structure of an AMO complex of the same family, Nitrosomonas europaea (Tucci et al., 2024). This study by Yang et al. is only slightly incremental compared to Tucci et al, as they manage to find the identity of the long transmembrane helix AMOD and to visualise a new AMOE short helical protein. The cryo-EM maps look nice, but the manuscript falls short of explanations and insights all through the text. The introduction could be better and more readable by explicitly explaining some concepts the are mentioned, but are not known by readers that are not in the field of mono oxygenates. As an example in line 6 the authors write “consisting 6 of three components and controversial copper-binding sites”, they could explain what this controversy is about. Does it have to do with the fact that in some of the pMMO structures Zn instead of Cu is found in the metal centers?
Regarding this, we have a major concern, how do the authors know that they have Cu rather than Zn bound in their structure? By EM density analysis they cannot be certain about it. We suggest to perform some sort of X-ray spectroscopy to identify the element. The authors mention in line 14 that O has been established to be a Cu dependent oxygenase, but there is no reference. This lack of citations is spread all over the text. It is hard to follow for someone that doesn’t know the specific literature.
The main text, results and discussion, is a description of the structure, but lacks completely functional analysis and argumentation about the role of certain observations. We consider and understand that in vitro biochemical characterisation of such en enzyme is very difficult, but some level of in-cell functional study should be possible and would make the paper more valuable. The authors could manipulate the bacteria strain to make a AMO-A tagged version. Is it not possible to include mutations in the various metal centres and then check the level N2O formation?
This would be really necessary to prove that the water path is important for e- transfer (as the authors state) and could be used to prove the physiological relevance of the double-copper presence at the Cu-D and Cu-C site.
Without any other type of assay, the structure analysis remains quite sterile, unfortunately.
The analysis of the lipids and their distribution is completely relegated to the supplementary materials, not attempt to identify the type of lipids has been done (e.g. mass spec?) and the lipids are not built in the deposited pdb. Why? We noticed that also the other group’s structure (Tucci et al. pdb-9cl6) doesn’t contain the lipids. On the other hand, very many water molecules were built in the maps, which is a bit surprising at this resolution. For some water molecules there is no density and for other water molecules the density is ambiguous and might also represent noise. The high-resolution noise and intrinsic motion of the outer side of the cryo-EM maps, makes it difficult to believe that all those H2O molecule can be built in the periphery of the structure. In the supplementary part about the methods the author are completely missing the description about model building. This should be corrected. We wonder whether the model was build starting from previous homologous structures that already included the waters. In any case the procedure that was followed to build the model should be described.
Going through the text:
- Page 3 Line 13: which are the two genes downstream of amoCAB that were considered accessory components of AMO in AOB?
- Page 4, line 6: what do the authors mean by “components”?
- As said before, mutagenesis of the key residues identified would be really useful to gain mechanistic information
- Page 8 Line 8an almost 4Å bond is labelled as H-bond this is a bit too far away
- Page 8 Line 16-17 The authors compare one TM helix in their complex with the correspondent one in pMMO. It would be useful to have a sequence alignment to see how conserved this helix is and if there are specific aa that would explain the kink of the helix.
- Line 8-12 page 9 the manuscript reads:
Close inspection of three coppers’ coordination environment reveals that a relatively weak hydrogen bond (Fig. 2b, e and f, red stars) consistently accompanies these coppers, suggesting their potential role in facilitating electron transfer during substrate oxidation, as previously reported, beyond merely stabilizing the copper site44-46.
How does the hydrogen bond network facilitate electron transfer? Could you please give a reference for such mechanism? Could the electrons not tunnel directly from metal center to metal center given that the distance is less than 20 Å? Do the authors maybe instead mean proton transfer to the active site?
- Page 9, line 15 the rod-shaped density could also represent noise instead of hydroxylamine
- Page 10 Line 1 it is confusing tha the bis-His site in introduced all of a sudden with no context, nor it was given in the introduction and with references lacking.
- Page 10 Line 14-16 . Notably, AmoD is positioned adjacent to AmoC with its N-terminal facing the cytoplasmic side and C-terminal oriented towards the periplasmic side (Fig. 1 and 3a).
Why notably? What is the functional implication of this observation?
And again on then following page The first alkyl chain of this lipid interacts with AmoD via Trp37 and penetrates into the hydrophobic core of AmoD and AmoC, while the second alkyl chain of this lipid anchors onto the surface of the TM1 of AmoC and stretches into the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane (Fig. 3c).
What are the physiological implications of such observation?

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Thank you for your letter and for the reviewers’ insightful comments on our manuscript
(Research Article, No. NCOMMS-25-30401). We greatly appreciate the time and effort

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In their manuscript titled "Structural insights into the catalytic mechanism of ammonia
monooxygenase", Yang and co-workers investigate the structure and mechanism of
ammonia monooxygenase (AMO). Ammonia oxidation is the critical first step of the
nitrification pathway within the global nitrogen cycle, converting ammonia to
hydroxylamine. AMO is an integral membrane metalloenzyme with high homology to
particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) and is of ecological relevance, as it
releases the greenhouse gas N2O, one of the main drivers of global warming, as a
byproduct.
The authors successfully determined the cryo-EM structure of AMO from a newly
isolated AOB strain, Nitrosomonas halophila ZJB1, at a resolution of 2.36 Å, yielding
a complete atomic model including sidechains and – more importantly – the
coordinated copper ions of the enzyme. The isolation and purification of the AOB strain
and subsequently the AMO complex are detailed in the supplementary materials,
including phylogenetic analysis of the isolated strain, the genetic engineering for
purification, and the cryo-EM sample preparation and data processing. The data as
presented seem sound and well processed, although the given initial number of particles
(ca. 320,000) seems low for 6,000 micrographs, given the quality of the micrographs
shown in Suppl. Fig. 2 and 3.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive assessment of our work and
insightful comments. The successful determination of the high-resolution structure of
the AMO complex in this study relied critically on the establishment of an effective in
vitro isolation and purification workflow using genetically engineered endogenous
tagging. We acknowledge that the current protein yield remains relatively limited,
which is partly attributable to the presence of multiple copies of AMO-encoding genes
in ammonia-oxidizing bacteria. Specifically, from approximately 120 liters of AOB
culture, we were able to obtain about 20 µL of highly concentrated, quality AMO
complex. As shown in the revised Supplementary Fig. 4, the particle concentration in
the cryo-EM samples was indeed relatively low, with only dozens of particles per
micrograph, ultimately yielding an initial particle set of approximately 380,000.
Despite this constraint, the genetic manipulation system and purification strategy we
developed provide a solid foundation for future structural and functional studies of the
AMO complex. We are confident that further optimization will enhance the yield and
facilitate more extensive investigations in this field.
Like pMMO, AMO is a cylinder-shaped homotrimeric assembly of heteropentamers.
Each protomer in the complex consists of five subunits: AmoA, AmoB, AmoC, a
recently discovered single transmembrane protein (AmoD), and a newly identified
extramembraneous subunit (AmoE). The core is composed of AmoA, AmoB, and
AmoC, with AmoB forming periplasmic β-barrel domains arranged counterclockwise
as a trimer. The structure is supported by 45 transmembrane helices contributed by each
subunit in each protomer. This is the second report on a structure of AMO, with the first,
at 2.8 Å resolution, determined in a native membrane environment by the group of Amy
Rosenzweig in 2024 (listed as reference 25). This work had already identified the
single-helix subunit that in the present work is now designated AmoD, but could not
identify the encoding gene due to a lack of resolution for the side chains. AmoD is a
single transmembrane protein positioned adjacent to AmoC, with its N-terminus facing
the cytoplasm and C-terminus oriented towards the periplasm. A similarly enigmatic
helical structure has been observed in particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO), a
related enzyme. Phylogenetic analysis suggests AmoD is exclusively present in the N.
europaea/N. mobilis lineage and its genomic location is associated with genes involved
in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and signaling molecule synthesis, leading the
authors to the interesting proposal that it plays a role in signal transduction during
ammonia oxidation. Two lipid molecules were observed embedded at the interface
between AmoD and AmoC.
In addition, the present work identifies AmoE as a further accessory subunit,
comprising two small helices and two flexible loops. AmoE binds to the positively-
charged surface of the N-terminal cupredoxin domain of AmoB through electrostatic
interactions. It also interacts with regions of AmoA and AmoC. Its genetic
neighborhood includes genes encoding components of ATPase and outer membrane
beta-barrel assembly machinery (BAM) complex. This led the authors to predict a
probable involvement in facilitating the assembly of the AMO complex within the cell
membrane. A speculative proposal, in particular because the connection of the (inner
membrane protein) AMO to the BAM machinery is not clear to this reviewer.
Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the
functional connection between AmoE and the BAM complex.
The structure of AMO determined in this study reveals that the newly identified AmoE
subunit is located on the periplasmic side of the complex. While the genetic
neighborhood of amoE includes genes encoding components of the ATPase and the
outer membrane beta-barrel assembly machinery (BAM) complex, we agree that the
functional implication of this genomic association remains unclear.
A recent cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) study of AOA, combined with cross-
linking mass spectrometry analysis of archaeal membranes, suggested a potential
spatial proximity between the extracellular S-layer and the AMO complex, which may
facilitate substrate uptake1,2. Although this does not directly clarify the role of AmoE,
it hints at possible functional interactions between ammonia-oxidizing enzymes and
outer membrane-associated components.
In light of the reviewer’s comment, we have toned down our interpretation and revised
the manuscript to reflect a more cautious hypothesis. We now propose that AmoE might
serve as a periplasmic adaptor, potentially facilitating structural or functional
communication across the periplasm—possibly helping to coordinate electron transfer,
metabolite channeling, or complex stability—without implying a direct role for BAM
in AMO biogenesis.
The revised statement now reads:
“In contrast, the genetic neighborhood of amoE encompasses genes encoding
components of the ATPase and outer membrane beta-barrel assembly machinery
complex (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 10a and c), suggesting a potential, though
still speculative, functional relationship. Given its periplasmic localization, we
hypothesize that AmoE may help coordinate interactions between the inner membrane-
embedded AMO complex and outer membrane-associated components, possibly
contributing to regulatory or substrate delivery processes. This is consistent with the
previously predicted interaction between the AMO and the S-layer outside the
membrane in archaea. However, further experimental validation is required to elucidate
its precise role.”
We thank the reviewer again for prompting this clarification, which has helped us
improve the accuracy of our discussion.
The high-resolution structure of AMO revealed a total of nine copper-binding sites,
with three per protomer forming two distinct copper centers. Interestingly, the dinuclear
His-site (somewhat confusingly) designated CuA in some studies on pMMO, is not
present in this AMO structure due to a substitution in the AmoB sequence, suggesting
less conservation. CuB is considered to be an electron transfer site in pMMO, although
a very similar site in the copper enzyme LPMO clearly is catalytic. In earlier work, the
nuclearity of CuB has been under debate, but more recent data on pMMO already
clarified its mononucler nature with the characteristic His-brace motif, and the present
data on AMO now confirms this unambiguously. The active site of AMO is suggested
to be at the CuC and CuD sites that feature a rather unique coordination environment
for copper by including hard oxygen ligands from side chain carboxylates or amides.
In AMO, the two sites form a second copper center with two simultaneously occupied

pMMO structures. These are nestled within a hydrophobic channel formed by

approximately 20 µL of purified AMO complex from 120 liters of Nitrosomonas

tag at the C-terminus of AmoA, ensuring that the tagged complex is expressed under
native regulatory elements. This approach maintains endogenous expression levels and
complex integrity, and the resulting purified complex is structurally and
compositionally representative of the native AMO. This similarity can also be

2. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis confirmed the presence of

recently reported AMO structure has included copper ions in the protein model, direct

of the purified AMO sample. The XPS results showed a weak but detectable copper
signal, with no indication of zinc (Response Figure 3). The low-intensity copper signal

copper ligands are deeply embedded within AMO and relatively low abundance of
copper in AMO (3 copper ligands per AMO protomer). Although the current
experimental technique and sample require further optimization, our results provide
direct evidence for the identification of copper in AMO.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Yang et al., report a structure of an ammonia monooxygenase enzyme (AMO complex)
from the ammonia-oxidising bacterium (AOB) Nitrosomonas halophila, and from a
new strain that the authors isolated themselves from mangrove sediments. They have
engineered a tagged version of the subunit Amo-A that they have used to isolate the full
complex that they have analysed by cryo-EM. At the end of 2024, another group also
obtained the structure of an AMO complex of the same family, Nitrosomonas europaea
(Tucci et al., 2024). This study by Yang et al. is only slightly incremental compared to
Tucci et al, as they manage to find the identity of the long transmembrane helix AMOD
and to visualise a new AMOE short helical protein. The cryo-EM maps look nice, but
the manuscript falls short of explanations and insights all through the text.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful assessment of our work. We are
pleased to highlight that our study provides several key advances beyond the structure
reported by Tucci et al. (2025), offering substantial new insights into the architecture
and mechanism of ammonia monooxygenase (AMO).
First, our structural analysis revises the oligomeric organization of AMO, revealing that
it assembles as a homotrimer of heteropentamers (each composed of AmoA, AmoB,
AmoC, AmoD and AmoE), rather than a heterotetramer. This refined architectural
model may have significant implications for understanding the complex’s stability,
catalytic function, and regulatory mechanisms, particularly in light of the proposed
functional roles of AmoD and AmoE inferred from their genomic contexts.
Second, we present the first direct structural evidence for the simultaneously occupied
Cu and Cu sites. Recent quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM)
C D
simulations have demonstrated that both Cu and Cu sites tend to maintain the Cu (I)
C D
active state, highlighting the potential relevance of a dicopper state; however, this state
had not been structurally resolved6. This finding of a dicopper center provides a
fundamental structural basis for understanding the diversity of the AMO active site and
the complexity of its catalytic mechanism.
Third, based on our high-resolution map, we propose a plausible proton transfer
pathway from Cu to Cu site within AMO, offering mechanistic hypotheses that can
B D
be tested in future functional studies.
Fourth, we identify pronounced differences in surface electrostatic potential between
AMO and pMMO, suggesting a structural basis for their distinct substrate selectivity
(ammonia vs. methane).
To enhance the physiological relevance of our structural findings, we have undertaken
several supplementary experimental investigations (please refer to the following text
for details):
1) We re-purified the AMO sample, collected additional cryo-EM data, and determined
a new AMO structure with the resolution of 2.59 Å, thereby confirming the presence of
water molecules and lipids, and enhancing the accuracy of the structural model;
2) We have identified the potential electron donor of AMO and may facilitate the
detection of enzymatic activity in future investigations.
3) We conducted X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to detect copper within the
AMO complex and to rule out the potential presence of zinc;
4) We carried out site-directed mutagenesis on key residues involved in copper
coordination, followed by enzyme activity assays to assess their functional roles;
5) We conducted lipidomics analysis on both the purified AMO sample and the newly
isolated AOB strain to refine the lipid modeling in the structural study.
We have fully revised the manuscript to improve clarity, emphasize mechanistic
insights, and better highlight these conceptual and experimental advances. We believe
our work provides a deeper and more accurate structural and functional understanding
of AMO that significantly extends beyond the current literature.

In direct response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we performed X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) analysis on our purified AMO sample. The results show a weak but
detectable copper signal, suggesting the presence of copper in AMO sample. No zinc
signal was detected throughout the measurement, indicating the absence of zinc in
AMO sample (Response Figure 3). The low intensity of the copper signal maybe
attributed to the following factors:
(1) Release of copper from AMO: To rule out interference from the copper ions in the
buffer as much as possible, we used the copper-free buffer to purify the AMO sample,
given the potentially low binding affinity of copper and AMO (binding energy > 930
eV), and the dynamic equilibration of copper between AMO and buffer, the copper
ligands are highly likely to release from the AMO during protein purification.
(2) Location of the copper ligands: The copper ions in our protein are deeply embedded
within the large, multi-subunit transmembrane structure. The sampling depth of XPS is
typically limited to 5-10 nm. Therefore, the photoelectrons (Cu 2p) generated from
these internal copper atoms are highly likely to be inelastically scattered and absorbed
by the surrounding protein matrix and lipid bilayer before they can escape the surface
and be detected.
(3) Low abundance of copper in AMO: The stoichiometry of copper in AMO complex
is relative low (only 3 coppers per AMO protomer). Consequently, the photoelectron
signal originating from copper is intrinsically weak compared to the abundant carbon,
nitrogen, and oxygen signals from the protein itself.
Although the current experimental technique and sample require further optimization,
our results provide direct evidence for the identification of copper in AMO.

corresponding to water molecules were consistently observed (Response Figure 9). This
result strongly confirms that these densities are not artifacts of noise. Additionally, the
placement of these water molecules is also supported by previously reported high-

3. Regarding model building:
We apologize for the omission of detailed model-building methods in the original
submission. The atomic model was built de novo using the cryo-EM map, the protein
sequence, and predictions from AlphaFold. The modeling process did not rely on
previously solved homologous structures, as no such structures were available at the
time. We have now included a comprehensive description of the model building,
refinement, and validation process in the Methods section as follows:
“Model building and refinement
The predicted AlphaFold structures of AmoA, AmoB, AmoC, AmoD, and AmoE were
manually docked into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF Chimera and subsequently
adjusted in Coot according to the corresponding density and sequence information.
Lipid molecules were selected based on lipidomics data and identifiable features, and
were manually fitted into the map using Coot. Water molecules within the AMO
complex, particularly those near copper centers, were modeled with reference to the
previously reported pMMO structure (PDB: 7S4H) and supported by mass
spectrometry data. Additional cytoplasmic and periplasmic water molecules were
placed based on the pMMO structure (PDB: 7S4H) and validated by the recently
published AMO structure (PDB: 9CL6). Real-space refinement and validation of the
final model were carried out using Phenix. Structural figures were prepared with UCSF
Chimera, ChimeraX, and PyMOL (http://www.pymol.org).”
We hope these revisions address your concerns and improve the rigor and transparency
of our structural analysis. Thank you again for your valuable feedback.

Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that the
presence of positively charged regions facilitating the transport of a positively charged
ion such as NH ⁺ appears counterintuitive at first glance. Below we clarify our
4
reasoning, which draws on electrostatic considerations, the biochemical properties of
ammonium, and a mechanistic precedent:
Electrostatic steering via alternating charge patterning:
The positive charges should not be considered in isolation; rather, they form part of an
alternating electrostatic motif along the membrane interface. In this model: Negatively
charged residues attract NH ⁺ ions from the extracellular milieu. Adjacent positive
4
residues help lower the energy barrier for ion permeation by electrostatically shielding
the NH ⁺ ion from subsequent repulsive negative patches, thereby facilitating a stepwise
4
“hand-off”. Thus, the positive charges serve not as direct attractors, but as facilitators
that mitigate electrostatic repulsion and reduce the dielectric barrier for ion
translocation.
Possible deprotonation of NH ⁺ to NH :
4 3
The ammonium–ammonia equilibrium (NH ⁺ ⇌ NH + H⁺) offers another plausible
4 3
mechanism. The local environment near the membrane—potentially modulated by
negative charges—could promote deprotonation, forming neutral NH . This uncharged
3
species would encounter no Coulombic barrier from positive patches and may diffuse
readily through hydrophobic regions. Reprotonation could subsequently occur near the
active site. In this scenario, positive surface charges help form a permissive path for
NH .
This electrostatic guidance mechanism may be analogous to that recently observed in
cation-translocating membrane proteins, the eukaryotic magnesium channel Mrs214,
where a charged vestibule facilitates the selective recruitment of cations from the
environment (Response Figure 12). This supports the idea that such an arrangement is
a functional and evolutionarily relevant feature in cation-translocating membrane
proteins.
In summary, we propose that the positive charges help form a dynamic electrostatic
network that guides NH ⁺ ingress—either via charge shielding or by permitting NH
4 3
diffusion. We acknowledge that further functional studies are needed to fully establish
the biological role of this electrostatic feature and have toned down speculative
conclusions accordingly.
